title_en: On the Incarnation and against the Arians
author: Marcellus of Ancyra
occasion: The author responds to opponents who, wishing to understand the divine Scriptures with evil craft, bring forward the human sayings of the Son's poverty to establish their own blasphemy. They ask how the Son can be like the Father or from the Father's essence, given texts about receiving life, being raised, being forsaken, and not knowing the last day.
argument: The humble sayings and experiences of Christ belong to his assumed humanity, not to his eternal divinity. The Son is by nature equal and consubstantial with the Father, and the Father acts through him in raising, sanctifying, and glorifying the incarnate Lord. The Holy Spirit is uncreated, of the same divinity and authority as Father and Son, and Scripture attributes the same works to all three, including creating, sanctifying, raising, giving life, speaking in prophets, and filling all things. Christ's human weakness and submission are the Church's own weakness and submission, so that in him humanity may be raised, glorified, and made children of God. The author therefore rejects any claim that the Son or the Spirit is a creature.

outline.move: The author introduces the opponents' proof-texts about the Son receiving life, being raised, and being forsaken, then explains that these refer to the Son's flesh and human nature.

He argues that the Son's lowly words and experiences are spoken for our sake and in his humanity, while as Word he is equal to the Father, and he interprets the rich young ruler and the unknown last day accordingly.
He expounds the exchange of sonship: the Son becomes son of Adam by the divine plan so that Adam's children may become sons of God, and he introduces the Spirit's uncreated divinity.

He begins the Trinitarian argument that Father, Son, and Spirit share one divinity and one Lordship, using the Spirit as living water, the seraphic doxology, and the Son's resurrection of his own body.
He explains that the Father raises, sanctifies, and glorifies the Son through the Son himself, and he accumulates scriptural evidence that the Spirit does the same works as Father and Son.
He continues the scriptural demonstration that the Spirit shares the divine nature, works, and glory, and that the three are one God, not a second God.
He interprets the Son's subjection and kingdom as the subjection and kingdom of his body, the Church, which is his assumed humanity.
He concludes by affirming from 1 John and the prophets that the crucified and risen Jesus is true God and true man, born of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God.

cast.name: Marcellus of Ancyra

The first portion or firstfruits, used of Christ's body as the first portion of the Church and of the Spirit as the first installment of our inheritance.
The temple, used of Christ's body and of believers as the dwelling place of God through the Spirit.
The full reality of deity dwelling bodily in Christ, in contrast to the partial gift of the Spirit in believers.

The Church, understood as Christ's body, the humanity he assumed and in which he is glorified and reigns.
Mediator between God and human beings, the role of the incarnate Christ as both God and man.

scripture: The author cites the Greek Old Testament, using LXX book names and Psalm numbering. In translation, use standard English Bible names and numbering: LXX Psalm numbers should be converted to Hebrew/English numbering where they differ. New Testament citations follow the Gospels, Acts, and Pauline letters by their traditional names.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is uncertain; the range c. 335–340 is approximate.
The original title is transmitted under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria, but the work is generally attributed to Marcellus of Ancyra; the attribution remains debated.
The precise identity of the addressee or original audience is not stated in the text.
The section divisions are editorial and may not reflect the author's original structure.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The author responds to opponents who, wishing to understand the divine Scriptures with evil craft, bring forward the human sayings of the Son's poverty to establish their own blasphemy. They ask how the Son can be like the Father or from the Father's essence, given texts about receiving life, being raised, being forsaken, and not knowing the last day.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ΤΟΥ ΕΝ ΑΓΙΟΙΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΗΜΩΝ ΑΘΑΝΑΣΙΟΥ ΑΡΧΙΕΠΙΣΚΟΠΟΥ ΑΛΕΞΑΝΔΡΕΙΑΣ, ΠΕΡΙ ΤΗΣ ΕΝΣΑΡΚΟΥ ΕΠΙΦΑΝΕΙΑΣ ΤΟΥ ΘΕΟΥ ΛΟΓΟΥ, ΚΑΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΑΡΕΙΑΝΩΝ.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source text is transmitted under the name of ATHANASIUS of Alexandria, not Marcellus of Ancyra. The opening title reads: 'Of our holy father ATHANASIUS, Archbishop of Alexandria, On the Incarnate Appearance of the God Word, and against the Arians.' The brief's attribution to Marcellus of Ancyra as author is not supported by the source text itself, which explicitly names Athanasius.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Marcellus of Ancyra — The author, bishop of Ancyra, writing against those who misuse Scripture to deny the Son's full divinity.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ΤΟΥ ΕΝ ΑΓΙΟΙΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΗΜΩΝ ΑΘΑΝΑΣΙΟΥ ΑΡΧΙΕΠΙΣΚΟΠΟΥ ΑΛΕΞΑΝΔΡΕΙΑΣ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source text identifies the author as ATHANASIUS, Archbishop of Alexandria. The name 'Marcellus of Ancyra' does not appear in the source text. The brief should list 'Athanasius of Alexandria' as the named author, with a note that modern scholarship attributes the work to Marcellus of Ancyra.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Luke — The evangelist who interprets the good gifts as the Holy Spirit and records Gabriel's announcement.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ὁ δὲ Λουκᾶς τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ἱστορῶν ἑρμηνεύει, τί ἐστι τὰ ἀγαθά, λέγων· Εἰ οὖν ὑμεῖς, πονηροὶ ὄντες, οἴδατε δόματα ἀγαθὰ διδόναι τοῖς τέκνοις ὑμῶν, πόσῳ μᾶλλον ὁ Πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς δώσει Πνεῦμα ἅγιον τοῖς αἰτοῦσιν αὐτόν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Luke is cited for interpreting 'good gifts' as the Holy Spirit (section 10), but the source does NOT say Luke records Gabriel's announcement. The Gabriel reference in section 13 states: 'καθὼς καὶ ὁ Λουκᾶς λέγει τὸν ἄγγελον Γαβριὴλ εἰρηκέναι πρὸς τὴν Παρθένον' — Luke says the angel Gabriel spoke to the Virgin. This is accurate. However, the description conflates two separate citations; the Gabriel announcement is not about 'good gifts' as the Holy Spirit.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Gabriel — Quoted as the angel speaking to the Virgin, sections: ['13']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καθὼς καὶ ὁ Λουκᾶς λέγει τὸν ἄγγελον Γαβριὴλ εἰρηκέναι πρὸς τὴν Παρθένον
_unresolved_facts.fix: Gabriel is NOT directly quoted in the source text. The text only reports that Luke says (λέγει) the angel Gabriel spoke to the Virgin. Gabriel's actual words are not cited; only a paraphrase of the announcement content follows ('Καὶ βασιλεύσει, φησίν, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα'). The speaker should be listed as 'reported speech about Gabriel' or removed from voices, since no direct quotation of Gabriel appears.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The rich young ruler — Quoted in the dialogue with Jesus, whose response is the focus, sections: ['4']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀπεκρίνατο λέγων· Ταῦτα πάντα ἐφυλαξάμην ἐκ νεότητός μου, τί ἔτι ὑστερῶ;
_unresolved_facts.fix: The rich young ruler is only partially quoted. The source text quotes Jesus's full response including the commandments, but the young man's reply is limited to 'Ταῦτα πάντα ἐφυλαξάμην ἐκ νεότητός μου, τί ἔτι ὑστερῶ;' The brief's claim that 'whose response is the focus' is misleading — the focus is entirely on Jesus's teaching about goodness and perfection, not on the young man's response.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ['1', '2']: 'The author introduces the opponents' proof-texts about the Son receiving life, being raised, and being forsaken, then explains that these refer to the Son's flesh and human nature.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ὅταν οὖν λέγει ὁ μακάριος Παῦλος, Ὁ Πατὴρ ἤγειρε τὸν Υἱὸν αὐτοῦ ἐκ νεκρῶν, Ἰωάννης ἡμῖν διηγεῖται, ὅτι ἔλεγεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον, καὶ ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις ἐγερῶ αὐτόν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 2 does not merely 'explain these refer to the Son's flesh.' It introduces major new arguments: that the Son as Life cannot receive life, that the Son as Wisdom cannot advance in wisdom, that the Father raises the flesh through the Son/Word, that the Son sanctifies himself for our sake, that the flesh is deified (ἐθεολογήθη), and Thomas's confession of 'the composite' (τὸ συναμφότερον). The outline oversimplifies section 2's content.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ['3', '4']: 'He argues that the Son's lowly words and experiences are spoken for our sake and in his humanity, while as Word he is equal to the Father, and he interprets the rich young ruler and the unknown last day accordingly.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οὕτως οὖν καὶ ὅτε λέγει, Κύριος ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ, περὶ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας λέγει, τῆς ἐν αὐτῷ κτιζομένης.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 3 contains a major argument not mentioned in the outline: that 'The Lord created me' (Prov 8:22) refers to the Church being created in Christ, not to the Son's creation. This is a crucial anti-Arian argument about Proverbs 8:22 that is entirely omitted from the outline summary.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ['6', '7']: 'He begins the Trinitarian argument that Father, Son, and Spirit share one divinity and one Lordship, using the Spirit as living water, the seraphic doxology, and the Son's resurrection of his own body.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο, ὥσπερ εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ βαπτιζόμεθα, οὕτως καὶ εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος, καὶ γινόμεθα υἱοὶ Θεοῦ, οὐ Θεῶν. Πατὴρ γὰρ καὶ Υἱὸς καὶ ἅγιον Πνεῦμα, Κύριος σαβαώθ ἐστι. Μία γὰρ ἡ θεότης καὶ εἷς Θεὸς ἐν τρισὶν ὑποστάσεσι.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 6 contains the explicit formula 'one divinity and one God in three hypostases' (Μία γὰρ ἡ θεότης καὶ εἷς Θεὸς ἐν τρισὶν ὑποστάσεσι), which is a major doctrinal statement. The outline's summary understates this — it is not merely 'begins the Trinitarian argument' but explicitly defines the Trinity. Additionally, section 7 includes extensive argument about the Son as Creator through whom all things were made, not mentioned in the outline.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ['14']: 'He interprets the Son's subjection and kingdom as the subjection and kingdom of his body, the Church, which is his assumed humanity.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τὸ λέγειν οὖν αὐτὸν, κάθου, ἀρχὴν σημαίνει· καὶ τὸ λέγειν, ἕως τεθῶσιν οἱ ἐχθροί σου, τέλος δείκνυσιν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 14 contains a significant chronological/grammatical argument about 'until' (ἕως) not implying the Son's kingdom ends, but the outline omits this. More importantly, section 14 includes the argument about two wills in Gethsemane (τὸ μὲν ἀνθρώπινον... τὸ δὲ θεϊκὸν) and Peter's rebuke as Satanic, which are major components not mentioned in the outline summary.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ['15']: 'He concludes by affirming from 1 John and the prophets that the crucified and risen Jesus is true God and true man, born of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ ὅτε λέγει ὁ Κύριος ἐν τῷ κατὰ Ἰωάννην Εὐαγγελίῳ· Αὕτη δέ ἐστιν ἡ αἰώνιος ζωή, ἵνα γινώσκωσί σε τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν Θεόν, καὶ ὃν ἀπέστειλας Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν· ἀλλαχοῦ ὁ αὐτὸς Ἰωάννης τὸν Υἱὸν λέγει ἀληθινὸν Θεόν· Οἴδαμεν γὰρ, φησίν, ὅτι ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ ἥκει· καὶ δέδωκεν ἡμῖν διάνοιαν, ἵνα γινώσκωμεν τὸν ἀληθινὸν Θεόν, καὶ ἐσμὲν ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ ἐν τῷ Υἱῷ αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ. Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς, καὶ ζωὴ ἡ αἰώνιος.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The outline says 'from 1 John' but the source cites the Gospel of John (τὸν κατὰ Ἰωάννην Εὐαγγέλιον) for 'that they may know you, the only true God,' and then cites 'the same John' (ὁ αὐτὸς Ἰωάννης) for 'the true God' in what appears to be 1 John 5:20. However, the source does not clearly distinguish these as separate works, referring to 'the same John' after citing the Gospel. The outline's '1 John' is an interpretive identification not explicitly marked in the source.
